cells.tense: You're at the bench right now, mid-build, no waiting for anyone's permission.
cells.ask: Name one thing you build that runs well, and say out loud what it asks of you to keep it that way. The naming hands back a truer hold on what's yours.
cells.core:
You're holding this up by tending it. You give the thing a shape and it keeps growing in that shape, and you can feel which parts are working and which need you today.

The work lands that way. You steer it, it stays alive, and when you look at what's here you don't have to talk yourself into being pleased with it. That's the proof this isn't luck. Two or three things are alive at once and you give them their water on the days they need it, not forcing days that aren't ready.

Ahead: let someone see what the upkeep asks of you, without that changing any of what you're carrying.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it growing by giving it a shape, and you own that.
cells.verb: keeping something alive by giving it a shape
cells.place: the part of a life that moves toward what it's aimed at

cells.tense: You're living a few weeks ahead, bracing for a version of this that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Take one piece that's actually finished — small counts — and set it down for a day without checking on it. Watch whether the grip was needed; many loads run better when nobody stands over them, and you find out which.
cells.core:
You're tending harder than the thing requires. Something isn't done, not exactly, and you keep working it — checking, adjusting, holding the whole plan in your head at once. Ahead of you there's a version where it all comes together, and you're doing today's work against that picture instead of against what's actually on the bench.

Tended well, this looks like steady hands and a long view — the work getting done because someone keeps showing up to it, not because anyone stands over it.

The trouble is that a thing can be going fine and still fail your inspection. So the work of tending has no finish. There's one more pass, and another, and the pass spends force the work already has. When you can't hand off or set down, some of the wear isn't the work — it's the grip.

Let one finished piece rest where it is. The rest is the part that tells you whether the grip was doing anything.
cells.sheetLine: Tending hard has become the work itself, and it's wearing you out.

cells.tense: There's a door behind you you're still standing at, waiting for it to open again.
cells.ask: Feed one thing you're excited about that isn't your duty — an evening on it, no ledger of progress. Watch one hour of what that gives you, and use it however it lands.
cells.core:
You want to be moving and something in you won't step. What's grown here has gone untended long enough that it stopped feeling like yours, and picking it back up would mean starting from a scrap. So nothing gets kept up, and the wait stands in for the moving.

Unforced, this is two or three things alive at once and you giving them their water on the days they need it — not all the time, but on the days that matter.

What's gone isn't the ability. What's gone is the link between caring about a thing and giving it your hours. Wanting to be somebody who builds and being that person have drifted apart, and drift doesn't close by pushing. Pushing at something gone quiet doesn't work — the quiet is the message, not the obstacle.

Water one thing that actually interests you, even if it becomes nothing more. The motion comes back before the confidence does.
cells.sheetLine: You still want this to grow. You've stopped giving it time.

cells.tense: You're at the wheel right now, moving this along, and not counting it as yours.
cells.ask: Say one sentence aloud, alone if that's easier: this is what gets kept alive, and it's mine. Let it land before moving on. That's where the next bit of momentum comes from.
cells.core:
You're holding this up right now — adjusting here, deciding there, doing it quietly enough that it looks like the situation is what moves. But the deciding is happening, and it's happening through you. The claim just hasn't been made.

Done well this is a steady hand nobody has to announce: a home, a team, a long project that stays on its feet because someone makes the small calls before they become big ones, without the gesture asking for credit.

The work of tending keeps running while the claim stays off. So you're the one keeping it alive and you describe it as though it runs itself. That's the move that pays you back — naming what you've been keeping steady costs nothing and puts the handle back in your hand.

Put it down in your own voice once and feel what that does. The work was already yours. The word is what's missing.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding this steady. Saying so is the piece that's missing.

attempts.check: The main unsupported claim to watch is any hint that the person has a history of exhausting themselves or of being unnoticed — the record says none of that, so the cells locate a position on a path and a condition of one capacity, not a biography. A reader might reasonably say 'I'm tired of building this, not failing to build it' — the Too Much and Unacknowledged cells hold both the wear and the genuine activity, without grading either. The asks survive being wrong because each one is a small act in the world that teaches the person something regardless: a done-thing named out loud, a finished piece of work set down, one movement fed through inspired feeling, one sentence telling someone what an effort cost. The sentence that would serve the writer more than the reader is the bright vision in Too Much — it is kept only to name where the pushing is headed, not to praise the vision itself.
